title: Elixir Examples
description: Each example belongs to one starter lesson. Follow its setup steps before trying it. These examples need the named tools and do not run in this site playground.

examples.title: Print a greeting
examples.description: IO.puts writes text and adds a newline. IO means input and output.

examples.title: Name a value
examples.description: A name can be bound to a value. The plus sign adds numbers.

examples.title: Name a fixed label
examples.description: An atom is a named label. It begins with a colon and is often used for a small set of choices.

examples.title: Keep a small group
examples.description: A tuple groups a few values. It is often used to return a status and a result together.

examples.title: Store a sequence
examples.description: A list holds a sequence of values. Enum.join turns these strings into one string.

examples.title: Use named fields
examples.description: A map stores key-value pairs. Atom keys can be read with dot syntax.

examples.title: Pull values from a shape
examples.description: The equals sign matches shapes and binds names to their parts.

examples.title: Choose with if
examples.description: if picks one of two branches. Only false and nil count as false in Elixir.
examples.code:
score = 8
IO.puts(if score >= 5, do: "Pass", else: "Try again")

examples.title: Use an anonymous function
examples.description: fn creates a function value. A dot is used when calling a function stored in a variable.
examples.code:
twice = fn n -> n * 2 end
IO.puts(twice.(4))

examples.title: Transform each value
examples.description: Enum.map builds a list using the result of a function for each item.
examples.code:
values = Enum.map([2, 3], fn n -> n * 2 end)
IO.puts(Enum.join(values, ", "))

examples.title: Read steps from left to right
examples.description: The pipe |> passes a value as the first input to the next function.
examples.code:
[4, 8, 9]
|> Enum.filter(fn n -> n >= 7 end)
|> Enum.sum()
|> IO.puts()

examples.title: Choose by a pattern
examples.description: case matches a value against patterns. _ is a catch-all pattern.
examples.code:
result = {:ok, 8}
message = case result do
 {:ok, n} -> "Score: #{n}"
 _ -> "Try again"
end
IO.puts(message)
